en: The Kaustubha on Vīraśaiva Conduct (Vīraśaivācārakaustubha) by N.A. Veerappa Moorthy.
Sanskrit manuscript written by hand on paper; no author (N.A. provided.
25 (398 Śloka) 13.5" x 8.4" Incomplete
Oṃ. The Vīraśaivācārakaustubha.
I am composing this Kaustubha for the illustrious Vīraśaiva dharma,
for the benefit of those great souls who are solely devoted to its practice. (1)
Salutations to the glorious one in embodied form, who is ever-exerting himself to protect the entire world;
whose conscious form is to be known through the composition of the playful splendor of the words of the Vedānta;
and who resides in the noble pavilion of the lotus-heart of his devotees steadfast in the heroic vow (vīravrata).
Homage, repeated homage, be to that Liṅga which is the light of consciousness, worthy of being perceived.
(2) His form is pure sattva, stainless like the kunda flower, the moon, or silver; he has accepted a woman as his left side, and is eager to ordain the welfare of the world through his grace.

May the Lord of Umā— who grants liberation from birth, old age, and death through the abundant grace of those possessing the extraordinary majesty of their wives' merit— shine before my mind. That Māyā, who is Nature (Prakṛti), though radiant with her own three qualities, remains unperceived by them individually.
Through the power of the magnificent display of the reflection of consciousness, the state of being the self of the universe is perceived.
May that auspicious Goddess Śivā, who gracefully sports with eyes rippling with blossoming compassion, bestow upon us all unimpeded prosperity, one after another. 4.

She whose intense devotion is the source of these [qualities], who has brought the Lord of the Gaṅgā under her own control, who is submerged in a series of waves from the surging ocean of her vast compassion,
and who is the teacher who proclaims the doctrines of the scriptures originating directly from the mouth of the Lord;

Therefore, may Nandīśa and Bhṛṅgīśvara bestow upon us a mere atom of the fortune of steadfast devotion. [May He be] Śambhu, whose body is lofty and inspires fear with its form of intense exuberance, manifesting a vast and throbbing *rājasa* quality that betokens surging indignation; and who is the abode of the splendor of heroes.

May Virabhadra, the lord of the Gaṇas, who dispels obstacles for me with his resolute roar during the act of threatening arrogant and wicked people through their association, destroy our impediments. (6) (p.3)
He who, having received the power of supreme intellectual skill from his father, has traversed the ocean of traditional lore;
who has rested upon the path of all Śaiva principles through the *Sat-kāmika* and other Āgamas;
and who, as the six-faced one (*Ṣaṇmukha*), has condensed [the teachings] into a small volume by means of those [texts] emerging from the five faces of the Goddess.
He clearly instructs his disciples and, for the sake of strengthening their understanding of the abandoned objects,
makes them concise. On the wall of our minds, I shall paint all the stainless, variegated forms of Hara and Hara—
those who dwell at the feet of the Lord on the radiant peak of Kailāsa— free from all duality.

To those who at all times perform service with a mind that surpasses their own self-interest, and who bow down to the face of Gaṇeśa—the knower of the six limbs—because it bestows all desired objects;
[to them], by the power of their own majesty, there is no fear of lightning on the earth. 8. New.

I bow to Basaveśvara, the preceptor of true Brahma-vidyā for those seeking liberation, who—acting as a treasure-house of compassion for the downtrodden—restrained the erosion of the shore; he who is once again the earth for the entire tree of the Vīraśaiva doctrine, flourishing like barley. (9)

O you who are weary on the path of Śiva, I contemplate that supreme Lord in my mind— He who is a watering station for the stream of nectar of the bliss of consciousness that uproots the mass of hymns [of worldly praise],
and who manifests as the destroyer of the mass of darkness of evil doctrines opposed to the path of liberation.
He who is known as Drākācandramas, the teacher of teachers to the gurus;
he who, having descended to earth, became the preceptor for the initiation into the Śaiva path for the Basavas,
and was born from the excellent womb of Dharmanāyikā, the consort of Vṛṣādhinātha.

May the source of the nectar of Brahman, who out of his playful human state is eager to remove the arrogance of the clamor of the wicked, swiftly bestow upon us the discernment between what is to be done and what is not to be done.
We bow to those renowned ones whose greatness for the sake of others is manifested through manifold successive acts.
I pay homage to those hosts of Mañjuśrīs, who, by means of establishing the lineage of the means for unbroken liberation,

have fulfilled the purpose of those whose intellects lacked clarity regarding the unseen reality— those who had fallen away due to the weight of their mental dispositions fashioned by various false doctrines. (12)
All knowledge is under one's own control, yet even that is rooted in the ignorance of the ego and its attendants;
it is tranquil, yet restless in its pursuit of the well-known state of Śiva which lies beyond all worldly desires.
The eight supernatural powers depend upon the mind, yet true accomplishment is found in the cessation of the manifold world through the realization of one’s own innate nature.
May the two feet of this [work], which possess the meter *gurubasavayati*, lead to the greatest welfare. (Let it be:
May the glorious city be a river of the waters of compassion, the sole sovereign of all that is supreme;
a bee at the lotus of truth, a delight to men, and possessing the skill of dancing peacocks.
The city of Bhavyāveṇu resounds with the continuous roar of Vedic chanting, which brings about the excellence of the self;
it surpasses the succession of all other cities on earth and in heaven.
There dwells the river of compassion for the king,
which has made the *ārī* lute its playful stream;
there arises that which is born in accordance with the love for the glory of the illustrious King Basava.
He is the golden mountain in his nobility, generosity, and steadfastness in the face of the wicked;
he is himself the stainless Lord of the Earth, whose crest is the Moon and who is the ocean of excellence.
He dwells in the mind of the one named Nirvāṇa with the effortless play of his own splendor.

Bearing the burden for the sake of favoring the world and for the restraint of those who hate righteousness, and providing assistance to this leader of the earth, the Lord of Vṛṣabha— the foremost among the illustrious Vīraśaivas— spreads joy throughout all the worlds. (16)
Possessing boundless and incomparable valor, he was one who bestowed wealth upon poets and others; his stride was unshakable and free from the disorder of Kali;
his mind was established in truth; and through his excellent ministers, he followed the path to liberation. (17)

O Noble One, your various qualities—fortitude, fame, excellent composure, majesty, profundity, and sweetness—are preeminent; having reached their full extent, they increase further at every moment. In him, these excellent groups of virtues exist together, mutually dependent, and are themselves infinite.
Through the asceticism of the world, he shone forth once more with the name Dhīra.
There was a renowned master named Bhadrappa, a preeminent jewel among lords and steadfastly devoted to the conduct of Śiva;
his son was the one called Nārappa, who possessed supreme virtues and a most excellent intellect.
In that ocean of his lineage, there arose a noble-souled master of mantras who was a divine jewel, a Śiva-liṅga;
he was a supreme gem of virtues upon the excellent ground of the land of Dāma, a powerful one whose very soil was love.
More beautiful than even Kandarpa, he was charming with the splendor of the excellent gifts emanating from his hands.

The beloved Lord Liṅgappa, who is like a majestic elephant, whose mountain-like temples are adorned with excellent pearl necklaces, who is as irresistible as the fierce elephant of the end of the eon, who is a Mount Mandara for those wishing to churn the ocean of deceit, and who is a Gaṅgādhara (Brahmā) to the learned masters of the Sindhurāgama; [to him] obeisance. 20.
Your arrow, O wretched one, does not bestow even a little life upon your enemies;
nor does it go to look for a friend in the abode of a virtuous treasury, remaining hidden there. Instead, having cast straw before your enemies, you steal away their fortune with your mouth.
If the enemy has arrived for battle, then he embraces him [in combat].
Where is the edge of the sword placed by the hand of Liṅgappaprabhu,
who is firm and fearless, while all his elephants and horses are armored and his enemies are struck down?
Even upon seeing the face of the enemy, which was filled with the tumultuous roar of kettledrums and cymbals,
you turned back from the battle in fear when you beheld the young grass placed [as a sign of surrender].
Generosity extends its activity toward both enemies and friends, gradually bringing about prosperity;

yet its stream sometimes burns the heart and at other times sprinkles it with the nectar of joy. Wonderful indeed, through its submergence in Indra-like power, that which is visible attains divine bliss.

Generally, the conduct of the virtuous is equal toward both enemy and friend. (23) Those two princes, whose forms were like those of the gods Kumāra and Māra, who possessed the qualities of the wise and the noble, and who were of excellent character, remained together with their guru.
The two [sons], Namra and Rājajaṅgama, were equal toward their own father and toward their kinsmen;
yet they were like two Arghinas who honored themselves among the forest-dwellers and the arrogant, ignorant folk.
Their elder brother was the renowned Basava Yati, whose name was Nirvāṇa, and who was possessed of great fame.

Renowned as Akkamma, she was the sister of one whose virtues were well-measured; she was a portion of fortune, distinct from the rest. She was the daughter of Tīta, who possessed exceeding prowess and had mastered all arts, virtues, and playful graces. She was the bearer of many noble lineages, her heart devoted solely to the fulfillment of her duties. (25)

In accordance with the king’s own command, his fame— desirable to all, moving like the crest-jewels upon the heads of many preeminent rulers such as the Bajarāyas— is exceedingly beautiful and skillful. It is the manifest ornament for the entire circle of kings, most exalted and delightful upon the earth.
The wise Alaṅgappanēta triumphs in this world through the playful pastimes of initiation and non-initiation;
having subdued Śiva by means of compassionate entreaties,
he brought about the destruction of the ego and was born as one free from all taints.
With the masses of staffs and caskets of Pracaṇḍa and others, he punished the circle of kings who had been humiliated; thus was the splendor of one named Nijāma proclaimed. 27.
He whose lineage of kings has met with defeat surely offers his respect to Liṅgappanetu with an abundance of love for the Lord. (28)
Day and night, delighting the earth with his prostrations,
he remained steadfast in his devotion to the worship of Maheśvara,
dwelling near Śeṣa by his command.
You explain all six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*) equally; and for more than a thousand assemblies of the *caramamūrti*,
you provide clothing and other gifts according to their mental dispositions.
They observed their own Vīraśaiva doctrine at all times through the worship of their chosen *liṅga*.
There exists a great sacred field (*kṣetra*) established by Kapila.
It is the abode for those seeking liberation from worldly existence and the refuge for those desiring enjoyment;
it is renowned as having transcended Kāśī, and it possesses a splendor resembling Mount Kailāsa. (31)
It shines, endowed with gurus who are devoted to the various glorious principles of Śaiva reality and accompanied by all those wise ones;
it is radiant under the name "Gurupura," which has achieved its own purpose.
It shines with countless houses born from dense thickets of trees;
outside here, those masses of pillars on both sides are hard.

The teachers here explain that [the self] is to be known through the non-discrimination of the distinct and sweet states [of consciousness]. However, one who is habituated to external conduct and whose character is like that of a mere man [merely] breaks his teeth when hearing this. (33)
The ocean, overflowing its bounds through the rising of the moon of his fame—
which is clearly heavy with joy— bows down with abundant devotion to this leader of the steadfast toward nirvāṇa, proclaiming it with his own mantras.
Accustomed to his own wife, he was shown the way by that river, which,
with its shimmering rows of broad waves acting as hands,
offered him heaps of pure, large pearls in the form of its abundant foam.
Day after day, with great devotion, Pañcasiṃhasamudra, remaining sleepless, recites the *Manu* [Purāṇa] while worshipping that preeminent sacred field;
they are bound together by a weight of mutual disparity.
These six seasons, headed by spring, abandon their enmity through a solemn oath; in that city, they quickly meet one another at the command of the Guru. (36)
One who dwells with a new guru attains the fruitfulness of birth;
when Kapila has attained oneness with the state of Śrīpada,
the entire fruit of birth becomes the very cause [of liberation].
It surely clarifies that [truth], and thus one approaches the feet of the Guru.
This sacred field (kṣetra), which cuts through the suffering of birth and death for people and is attainable only by those who disregard the accumulation of merit, [is now reached]. 37.
Śambhu shines in the form of Kapi-siddha-svāmī— the wish-fulfilling cow for all poets of pure words, and the ten-million-fold sun for dispelling the darkness of the impurities of the Kali age.
Though free from longing, the Lord of Dharma, whose minister is Nirvāṇa, daily celebrates with infinite, inexhaustible, and world-illuminating blessings countless festivals for him. (39)
In the month of Māgha, during the great festival celebrated with the assembly of the Śaiva community and the practice of Śiva-yoga,
people [gather] for the sake of achieving their respective goals.
Having traveled from region to region,
the minister of Nirvāṇa, together with the assembly of citizens, announced [the matter] to his own king by means of a request for permission.
Liṅgappanetā, together with his wife, set out with a white umbrella and a fourfold army;
he approaches the perfected sage Kapila.
In their minds, they offered salutations with a weight of devotion; through the medium of hymns from all the Tantras and Vedas, they performed praise playfully. 42.
Thereafter, during the great festival for the worship of his lotus-feet,
no obstacle was perceived by him who had already perceived [the truth].
For embodied beings who possess internal devotion,
when the sprinkling of fruits and other offerings is performed ten thousand times upon the feet and the head, the celestial river [Ganges] previously situated in the sky descends there.
"O two who conquer enemies, enter into the state of being my parents-in-law; a festival has commenced every day. 44.
A festival has begun that continues day after day.
At every moment, [my mind] is ever-new toward the lotus-feet.
7) This folio is not available.
May your speech, through its graceful charms, cause our heart-lotus to bloom until the end of the aeon. 53.

Having taken as his support that supreme human goal— the truth which removes the marks of worldly existence— for the benefit of the world and for the sake of favoring me, he who desires to know this [truth].
O you who have attained silence, may you awaken us!
O you whose intellect shines with the dawn of logic, quickly explain the words of Śruti;
O you who are the author of all Vedānta, speak of the perfect harmony between the indicative marks, the limbs [of the ritual], and both together.

"In the exposition of the true nature of words through their various distinctions, and in the commentaries on the Śrīpāṇinīya system and the ancient and future Vīraśaiva traditions, [he is] the author of the *Tattvārtha*.
(55) Thus, having accepted this command upon his head,
The minister Liṅgapra,
whose inner heart was awakened by the grace of the Lord, explained the meaning as it had been revealed to the sovereigns. (56)
Having realized the truth taught in all the scriptures, and being free from doubt, he,
together with his ministers, [strived] for his own welfare and for the sake of the benefit of all beings.
There, having first performed a prostration before the assembly of the *jaṅgamaliṅga* [wandering ascetics],
the minister Liṅappa took his seat and worshipped them with devotion.
By means of many flowers of speech, characterized by clear and sweet sentiments and serving as the sowing of seeds for the prosperity of the entire world,
that Brahman was offered into the lotus-pond of the heart within Rāma, who is delightful to the self.
The body is a temple; within the hollows of the two ears, you deposited the mantra.
Regarding the reality of the six auspicious marks (*satka-ti-liṅga*), you have honored [the lineage] with the thought, "I am the son and disciple.
By you, who possess vast majesty, seven lineages were established at the very beginning. (58)

Uṣā is the lineage of the *sāttvika* type, while Pacalitā is the lineage of the *rājasī* type; she is the cause for the *sāttvika* lineage as well, being sixfold and even more excellent than Sītā. However, through your grace, I have attained modesty, but not the form of Śiva.
"In the mirror of whose speech these meanings are reflected for all time"—
as the illustrious Liṅgaṇa, the ornament of his noble family, was speaking thus and requesting a work of merit,
the teachers then chose him and fulfilled his desired aim.

Seeing me standing at his side, he who desires the welfare of the world asked me, who had been honored and whose purpose was proclaimed, about my practice; then, out of compassion, he placed his hands upon his chest and his head. (61)
May the incomparable wisdom of the illustrious Maunappa be bestowed upon you through his graces— wisdom that,

by its very nature of liberation, brings benefit to all people. May all [these works] attain the status of celebrated meritorious deeds for us through the instruction of Dhīraliṅgappanetu, who is greeted with universal acclaim.

"Let the work of the wise, which brings forth the goal of the virtuous man, endure for no small duration until the end of the kalpa"— this command of the moving beings, which captivates the hearts of the truly learned, was uttered from the mouth of Amṛtabhū, who immediately moved with grace, by means of collections of appropriate verses composed by someone.
It possesses a disposition free from the pride of various doctrinal designations, recollections, and conclusions;
it expresses the purport of the meaning of the glorious divine scriptures (divyāgama) in accordance with Vīraśaivism;
and it is filled by the nectar of the light of grace from the two eyes of the glorious Jaṅgama.

May this speech, which has arisen from the heart of the one whose purpose is the mountain of glorious majesty (Śrī-Mahimālaya), and which is like the sun; which is praised by the swans—the wise who dwell at the holy ford of the six sites (Ṣaṭsthalatīrtha); and which is the battle-cry of the minister Liṅappa—may it sprinkle the hearts of the learned for all time. 64.
At the time of the dance on Mount Kailāsa and other places, surrounded by Brahmā and the other gods,

Śiva seated Śarvāṇī in the auspicious pavilion and made her his witness to the dance. Then, for the purpose of commencing the performance, he respectfully took up the conch and other instruments, while Ānandī and others held their positions.
"May this form of mine become worthy of being beheld even once.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of One's Chosen Deity, the Lineage, and Other Matters," in the *Kriyākāṇḍa* of the *Vīraśaivācārakaustubha*, composed by Maunappa Vidvan—who was born from the lotus-hand of the venerable teacher Canna Vīrasvāmī, the preceptor of Vīraśaiva initiation; who attained full realization through the grace of the eminent Guru Basava Yati, the foremost of teachers who pierced the veil of ignorance regarding the knowledge of the six *sthala*s transmitted through the beginningless lineage of the *Pramatha*s.
The Second Chapter.
Listen attentively, O Liṅgappaneta!
This is the science of all things, which accomplishes every purpose.
Even Śiva is swiftly attained;
may he sprinkle me with the nectar of his side-glances.
[1] She whose nature is the excellence of intellect that has vanquished even the preceptor of the gods...
Resembling a formidable adversary, with the prosperity of his arms as fragrant as a celestial tree—
O Minister Liṅgappa, you alone are blessed upon the surface of the earth,
since such upright intellect and noble conduct have arisen within your hearing.
Therefore, for those who possess clear renown,
there would be no extraction of the truth for anyone without inquiry, even until the end of the kalpa.
Consequently, having thoroughly mastered knowledge, one should investigate its objects.
And that is the Vidyoddeśa-tantra; I shall teach that Vidyā to you.

Having heard the Vidyās in their proper order and having found delight therein in their true meaning, and with your mind established in that doctrine, you will attain the state of being free from all distress.
The limbs [of the Veda] are four: Mīmāṃsā, Nyāyavistara, Purāṇa, and Dharmaśāstra; these are the fourteen branches of knowledge (vidyā).
Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, and likewise Jyotiṣa.
Chandas and Jyotiṣa—these are said to be the six limbs of the Veda.

(8) The Ṛgveda is considered to have twenty-one divisions; the Yajurveda is held to consist of one hundred branches; the Sāmaveda has a thousand divisions, and the Atharvaveda is recorded as having nine. (9)
The Vedas consist of two sections according to the distinction between what they teach:

therein, first is the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa), and following that is the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa). Each branch [of the Veda] should be understood as consisting of these two, including the Upaniṣads.
The Śrī Rudra, Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Śvetāśvatara, and Muṇḍaka; the Kaivalya, Kālāgnirudra, Kaṭhavallī, and Bāṣkala;
as well as the Haṃsa, Paramahaṃsa, and both the Brahmanārāyaṇa [Upaniṣads]. (11–12)
The Rāma-tāpanīya, the Pūrva- and Uttara-tāpanīya, the Gopāla-pūrva- and -uttara-tāpanīya, followed by the two Tāpanīyas known as Nṛsiṃha,
and finally the Pūrva- and Apara-tāpanīyas beginning with the Veṅkaṭeśvara.
The Pūrvottara-tāpanīya, followed by the Kūrma;
then, in sequence, the Yogaśikhā, Dīpaśikhā, and Liṅgopaniṣad;
the Kātyāyanī, Brahmabandhu, Āruṇi, and Amṛtabindu. (14–15)
Pañcabrahma, Jābāla, Tejobindu, Maudgala, Bodhāyana, Carca, Śravaṇa, and Parākrama. (16) (p.11)
The Prācyaśva, the Śaunakīya, and the Śivasaṃkalpa; the Āśvalāyana, the Maitrāyaṇīya, and the Vājasaneyaka;
as well as the Vedāntasārapravaṇa, the Vajrasūcī, and the Bāṣkala. (17)
The Sāṃkhyāyana, the Chāndogya, and also the Bṛhadāraṇyaka;
the Taittirīya, the Aitareya, the Praśna, the Garbha, and the Anu;
the Śarabha, the Atharvaśikhā, and the Nirlepa, as well as the Ādiccidambara.

The *Nirālamba-mahāvākya*, the *Mahopaniṣad* in its sequence, the *Pañcīkaraṇa*, as well as the secret narrative of the *Śruti*, the *Sūtra-siddhānta-śikhā* and other principal works, and the systems of *bhakti-yoga* and so forth are thus considered. (20)
The *Sattvasaṃkhyākopaniṣad* is said to be the latter section (*uttarakāṇḍa*).
Mīmāṃsā is considered to be twofold, through the division into Pūrva and Uttara. The Vaiśeṣika system of Kaṇāda and the Nyāya treatise are likewise considered to be twofold. (21–22)
Īśāna, the wise one, is the teacher of all sciences and the primordial Guru.
His disciple was Mahāviṣṇu, a great ocean of all knowledge. From whom [did he receive] the complete realization? [From] Brahmā, the teacher of the entire world.
The blessed Sanatkumāra heard this from Brahmā.
Sanatkumāra is omniscient, and the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana has attained all higher knowledge; from him this was heard by me.
Even today, the world of the gods exists with an extent of one billion [yojanas].
This [work] has been condensed by the supreme seer for the benefit of the world.
These four hundred thousand [verses] were proclaimed by Vyāsa, whose deeds are manifest.
Then, having divided it into eighteen parts and established their respective meanings,

he composed the narrative known as the *Bhārata*. Indeed, by way of enumeration, these five [books], including the supplementary portion (*khila*), are proclaimed to contain five hundred thousand and twenty-five thousand [verses] as their sacred measure.
And that supreme narrative of Rāma which was proclaimed by Vālmīki—
originally spoken by Brahmā with an extent of one hundred crores [of verses]—
was first told by him to Nārada, and by him again to Vālmīki.
And by Vālmīki, this unsurpassed [work] was revealed to the worlds.
Consisting of twenty-four thousand [verses], it bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
I shall now briefly state the names of the Purāṇas and so forth in their proper order.
Listen with a mind endowed with devotion, O crest-jewel of ministers:
first the Brāhma Purāṇa, then the Pādma, and indeed the Vaiṣṇava.
The Śaiva, the Bhāgavata, the Bhaviṣya, the Nāradīya, the Mārkaṇḍeya, and the Brahmakaivarta should be known;
as well as the Laiṅga, the Vārāha, the Skānda, and the Vāmana. || 33 ||
The Kaurmya, the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and immediately after that the Brahmāṇḍa—
these eighteen Purāṇas have been declared in their proper order.
Among these eighteen Purāṇas, Śiva is described by ten.
The Lord Viṣṇu [is the author] of four Purāṇas, Brahmā likewise of two, Agni of one, and Āditya of one; thus the Purāṇas are divided according to their respective portions:
the Śaiva, Skānda, Laiṅgya, Kaurma, and Vāmana.
O Sage, the ten Śaiva Purāṇas are the Vārāha, the Bhaviṣya, the Mātsya, the Mārkaṇḍeya, and the Brahmāṇḍa. Likewise, the Nāradīya, the Bhāgavata, and the Gāruḍa are the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas. (37–38)
O Pot-born One, these four are the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas:
the Brāhma, the Pādma, the Brahmakaivarta of Viṣṇu (the Creator), and the Āgneya of Agni; thus, O Sage, are the Purāṇas [enumerated] in order.
Next, I shall describe the Upapurāṇas in their proper order:
first the Sanatkumāra-ukta, then the Nārasiṃha; after that, the Sandhisaujña, which was narrated by Kumāra.

The fourth is the Purāṇa called Śivadharmākhya, narrated by Nandin; after that, the one spoken by Dūrvāsas, and following that, the Nāradīya. Then there is the Kāpila and the Mānava, as well as the one told by Uśanas.
Then follows the Brahmāṇḍa, which is highly meritorious and known as a Purāṇa.
After that is the one called Kālīpurāṇa, and the one named Kālakaṇṭha.
Then there is the one known by the name Vāsiṣṭhalaiṅga, and that which is called Māheśvara.
Then [he recited] that which is called the Sāmba Purāṇa, the Sāvitra, as proclaimed by Parāśara, the pure Mārīca, and that named Bhārgava;
the Mahābhārata, along with its various Itihāsas, in their entirety.
Romaharṣaṇa related it to all the sages:
"That Vārata [Mahābhārata] should be known as consisting of eighteen books, including the Ādi-parva, the Sabhā-parva, and likewise the Āraṇyaka-parva. (46–47)
The Virāṭa Parvan is to be known as the fourth, and immediately after that, the Udyoga Parvan; following that is the Bhīṣma Parvan. (48) (p.
The seventh is the Droṇaparva, and the eighth is the Karṇaparva;
the ninth is the Śalyaparva, and after that follows the Gadāyuddha (Club-fight).
Following that, the Sauptika (Night-attack) is proclaimed, as well as the Aishīka (Arrow-shower) and the Garbhapātana (Feticide).
The thirteenth is the Strīparva, and that of the slaying of the demon Madaka;

The listeners of this Ajita [Tantra] heard it from Śiva, who is named Suśiva:

it consists of twelve parts of the sun and moon, eight elephants, three fires, two pairs, desire, the seasons, and the eyes;
and finally, it is joined with the digits, the sages, the days, the digits, the fires, and the oceans.
The divisions of the Āgamas are [calculated] by the worlds (14) multiplied by the suns (12), with the ears (2) added;
[thus they are] 282. The Uttara, the Nārasiṃha, and also the Bhairavottara.
The experts in the Tantras have proclaimed three divisions of the Kāmika:
the Vīṇā, the Śivottara Tantra, the Sūta, the Saṃtāna, and the Sāra; and that which is known as the Ātmayoga is the fifth division of the Yogaja. 101–102.
The destruction of evil arising from others, the well-considered, the blissful, and the immortal—

Mahendra, Pāvaka, Dairghya, Māraṇa, and Bhīmasaṃhitā.

Enmity and cause— these are remembered as the sevenfold causes. The *Pārvatīśa*, the *Parodbhūta*, the *Prabhūta*, and the *Padmasaṃhitā* are the four divisions of the *Ajitatantra* proclaimed by those who have mastered the tantras.

Then, from that [bliss], there arose the immeasurable, inexhaustible, and unborn bliss of the one of infinite splendor, known as Mādhava, Uddhava, and Matsya; for that indeed was the manifestation of the Infinite.
Of the radiant [state], there are nine divisions, while of the subtle, there is but one division.
It is past, stainless, pure, immeasurable, and easily understood.
It reveals the distinctions of the [spiritual] lineages and awakens one to the ornaments of the system of awakening.
Thus, there are ten divisions of the tantra known as the Thousand. 106–107.
The Kāśyapa, Vāsava, Brāhma, Gaitama, Nīlalohita,
Vidyāpurāṇa, Vāsiṣṭha, Bhūtatantra, Mahendraka, Ātmālaṅkāra, and the section known as Īśānottara. (108)
The divisions of the twelve-rayed [Sun] are the Suprabheda and Abhedaka;
Mṛtyunāśa, Bhava, Saumya, Kaubereśa, Madodbhava, Aghora, Mahāghora, and Vijaya—thus the Vimala is eightfold. (110–111)
Niśvāsa, Ghoraniśvāsa, Niśvāsanayana, Sudhā, Niśvāsottara, Kūla,
Niśvāsavadana, and Udaya— these are the eightfold divisions of the Niśvāsa, distinguished by the various types of Niśvāsakarika.
The lotus of Prajāpati’s doctrine and that of Svāyambhuva—thus it is threefold.
This is the Ājñā [cakra], and the one known as Vyoma (Space) is twofold; the Āgneya (Fire) is established there.

Amoha, Mohasamaya, Śakaṭa, Śākaṭāyaka, Vilekhana, Vimala, Hala, Bhadra, and Vīraka. (115)
Thirteen divisions of the Vīratantra have been proclaimed:

[These include] the *alaṅkṛta*, the *bhīmaraudra*, the *aṭṭahāsa*, the *vṛṣodara*, the *ārevata*, the *atikrānta*, the *vṛṣapiṅga*, and the *subhadraka*. (117–118)
Ākrānta, Arcita, Bhoga, the one called Ananta, Māraṇa, Vṛṣaguhya, Sudatta, and Vimala— these are the sixteen [pīṭhas].
Also Ekapādapurāṇa, Sthāṇvākhya, and Nandikeśvara.
The Śrīmukha, the Vāyavya proclaimed by Śaṅkara, the Śivaśāsana, the Śivabhadra,
the Kalpabheda, the Vāraṇa, the Śivasekhara, the Devīmata, and the Sthiravyāpta— these are the fourteen [tantras] in the Candrajñāna. || 120–121 ||
The Ārdhālaṅkāra, Aiśāna, Pratibimba, Mayayoga, Kauṭaka, Kaṭinīra, Kuṭṭima,

Kālajñāna, Dhanurveda, Āyurveda, Dhanurdhara, Vijñāna, Akuśa, Gīta, Ātodya, and likewise Bharata;

Anila and Śāṃkara constitute a pair; thus, it is considered sevenfold within the Santāna lineage.
The Īśāna, the Śivadharma, and likewise the Śivadharmottara;
that which was composed by the Goddess, the Saumya, and that spoken by Śarva—these are remembered as the fivefold [collection].
Also included are the Samānya, the Sākṣin, the Haṃsa, the Mataṅga, and the Suprayogaka.

Śarva, Sarvātmaka, Śuddha, Śreṣṭha, Rudra,
Parohita, and Vātulottara— these twelve are recorded as the Vātula-saṃhitās.
Thus, all these saṃhitās number two hundred and eight.
Thus, there are fifty-eight divisions of the Śaivas known as the Raudras.
It is declared that there are one hundred and fifty divisions of the eighteen types of Rudras.
Likewise, there are the Vaināyakas, the Śāktas, the Kapālas, and the Sāras.
The Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist, and Śaiva systems are declared to be the six philosophical schools (ṣaḍdarśana).
The wise should know the Vaināyaka as a quarter, while they understand the Kaṭa-Śākta as another.
The Kāpāla is said to be the belly, whereas the Sāraka is the chest.
The Skanda, the Vaiṣṇava, and the Śaiva are likewise remembered as the heads;
the six systems of philosophy are proclaimed as the six limbs of the body.
The Yana, the Dūṣya, and the Himāṅga are all-purifying.
"O destroyer of faults, grant me such a limb as that!
Even though he is my devotee, he does not know the Śaiva tradition when confronted with one who seeks to harm him.

Parārdha, lakṣa, and also lakṣakoṭi; from that, yuta, prayuta, and padma;
in the śaṅkhas, lakṣa, nalina, and two koṭis.
One *koṭi* is half of two *kāṭīs*; a thousand *nadīs* is a *niyuta*; an *arbudha* is [the same];

six thousand and one hundred thousand. (140)

Śamba, Parārdha, Kamalārbudodha,
Vyomārkakoṭi, Gajasindhulakṣa,
and Bhūtāgnisāhasra— thus they are declared.

The ocean is the last and the middle [is the first].

Mahocchuṣka, Vātula, and Vātulottara. (146)
Hṛdbhedam, Ātmabhedam, Guhyatantram, and Kāmikam;

Mayottaram, the one called Vīṇā, Krokalam, and Krokalottaram. (147–148)
The *Pañcāmṛta*, the *Rūpabheda*, the *Bhūtoddāmaratantra*, the *Kalāsāra*, the *Kuloddīśa*, and likewise the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*;
the *Sarvajñānottara* and the great *Mata* as well. (149)
The Mahālakṣmīmata, the Siddhayogīśvarīmata,
the Kurūpikāmata, the Rūpikāmata, the Sarvavīramata, and the supreme Vimalāmata. (150–151)
The eastern, western, southern, northern, and unsurpassed [directions] are there;
one should know the Vaiśeyaka [region], and after that, the Vīrayoga.
Then there are Aruṇeśa, Mohaneśa, and Viśuddheśvara.
The Sarvavīramata and the supreme Vimalāmata;
(153) thus are these tantras, as well as many others in great number.
Now, there are also eighteen hundred Vaiṣṇava tantras. (154)
Among those numbered one hundred and eight, the Pādma, the Pādmodbhava, the Trailokyamohana, the Viṣṇutileka, and the one called Kanaka are considered [the best]. (Māyāvaibhava, Nalakūbara). 155.
The Nāradīya, the Lānadīya, the Vāsiṣṭha, the one called Puṣkala, the Sanatkumāra, the Sanaka, the one named Satya, and the Viśvasaṃhitā. (156)
The great inquiry known as Sānanda, the inquiry concerning women, and the Puruṣottama;
having recited the Mahendra-saṃhitā, which is an ocean of ultimate inquiries;
the Vāsiṣṭha, the Sātvata, the Rejo, the Draviṇa, and that called Śrīkara.
The *Sāṃvarta*, the *Viṣṇusadbhāva*, the *Siddhānta* preceded by Viṣṇu;
the *Viṣṇutattva*, the *Kaumāra*, the secret [text] preceded by Viṣṇu; the *Viṣṇuvaibhavika*, the *Tāra*, the *Saumya*, and the *Īśānasaṃhitā*. (158–159)
The Pūtantra, the Śaunakīya, the Mārīca, the Dakṣasaṃhitā, the Aupendra, the Yogahṛdaya, the Hārīta, the Pārameśvara,
the Ātreya, the Mandira, the Viṣvaksena, and that which is called the Auṃśa. (160)
The Vaihāyasa, the Vihangendra, the Hārṣa, and the Paramapauruṣa;
the Yājñavalkya, the Gautamīya, the Paulastya, and the Śākalāhvaya; the Jñānākhya, the Jāmadagnya, the Yāmya, and the Nārāyaṇātmaka. (161–162)
The Pārāśarya, the Jābāla, the Kāpāla, the one called Vāmana, the Dayottara, the Bārhaspatya, the Jaimini, the one called Sātvata,
the Kātyāyanīya, the Vālmīka, and the Maupagāyana-saṃhitā.
Hiraṇyagarbha, Āgastya, Kārṣṭya, the one named Bodhāyana, Bhāradvāja, Nārasiṃha, Gārgya preceded by Uttama,
Śārāta, Aṅgīrasa, Kāśyapa, and the one named Paiṅgala. (164–165)
The Trailokyamohana-yoga, the Nāradīya, the Vāraṇa, the Kṛṣṇacāmara-ajñeya, the compendium of Mārkaṇḍeya (166),
the one called Mahā-sanatkumāra, the one called Vyāsa, and the Viṣṇu-saṃhitā.

The Mārkaṇḍeya, the Pārśada, the Brāhma, and the Naraka-saṃhitā; the dialogue between Kadrū and Śukrā, the one called Umā-Maheśvara, the Dattātreya, the one called Śarva, and the one called Vyāsa—these are the names. (167–168)
Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Vāmana, Kalki, Rāghava,
and the one called Prācetasa— these are the hundred and one [Tantras] that have been heard.
These names of the Tantras were declared in their proper sequence by the ancients.
Thus, one hundred and one Vaiṣṇava tantras are spoken of.
There are sixty-four Śaiva tantras and many others as well. However, the authority belongs to those tantras that conform to the Vedas, while the others [do not].
The Nigamas and Āgamas are indeed non-Vedic; yet there is identity between the Vedas and the Siddhāntas because they propound the same meaning. (172)
The wise should always understand the authority of these two to be equal;
or rather, those Śiva-āgamas have issued directly from the mouths of Śiva himself, as heard by us from his breath. (173) They are superior because they have emerged directly from the mouth of Śiva.
The Nigamas and Āgamas spoken by Śiva have mutually non-contradictory meanings;
it is only those of small intellect who imagine a contradiction between them.
For the Nigamas and Āgamas are the instructions of the Supreme Authority. (174–175)
The authority [of these scriptures] should be understood without distinction by those who perceive reality—that which is proclaimed by human sages, gods, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others.
Each subsequent one possesses a superior excellence, while each preceding one serves as its instructor. (176)
Thus it is expounded in the principal treatises such as the *Kriyāsāra*.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Instruction on Vedic and Non-Vedic Knowledge," in the section on Ritual Action (*kriyākāṇḍa*) of the *Śrīvīraśaivācārakaustubha*.
The Third Chapter.

O foremost among the ministers of signs, O learned one, from the instruction of the knowledge taught in the Maunaprapanna [Tantra], which is higher than the highest, tell me that from which the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings manifests. [1] O learned one, according to the Kāmika-kalpa.
O True Lord, listen specifically to that which has been created by you.
From such authoritative sources as, "The Lord of all sciences, the teacher of Śarva and others, O wise ones," Śiva is remembered as the Sovereign of Knowledge (Vidyādhipa). || 3 ||
In this manner, the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings manifests; hear that now.
The glorious, great, primordial devotee, self-luminous and secondless—he who is proclaimed as "Brahman" by those who know the true meaning of the principle of Śiva.
Therefore, he who appeared as the stainless moving one (the Jangama) [is Śiva]. From his crest-lock (śikhā), the Linga of Emptiness (Śūnyaliṅga), the cause of the universe, was born.
From that, moreover, by his own will, the partless Linga (Niṣkalaliṅga) was produced.
From that partless *liṅga*, however, the *Mahāliṅga* itself arose;
from that, the *Praṇavaliṅga* was born at the beginning of creation.
From this [arose] the *Śivatatva*, and from that, the *Sādākhya*.
From him Maheśvara was born; from him Rudra originated.
From him Janārdana was born; from him the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) was born. (8) (p. 22)
This entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, has arisen from the Grandfather (Brahmā).
First, I shall describe in due order the characteristics of the beginningless devotee.
That which exists is the Supreme Brahman; that from which [the world] arises is itself the Soundless (Anādin).
Therefore, those who know the truth have declared that this devotee is beginningless;

the *liṅga* and the *jaṅgama* are designated as such, and the devotee is of an eternal, beginningless form. (11) That which is called the *liṅga* is the *liṅga*, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is said to be the *jaṅgama*.
A devotee is said to be one whose essential nature is the unity of the *liṅga* and the *jaṅgama*.
The *jaṅgama* is of the form of the *liṅga*, and the *liṅga* is of the form of the *jaṅgama*.
This union of the *liṅga* and the *jaṅgama* is the characteristic of a true devotee.
The devotees of the *liṅga* and the *jaṅgama*, though three in number, are indeed of one single nature.
When the body and the vital breaths have arisen, there is the determination of renunciation and lineage.
That which is eternally full, consciousness-bliss, and of the nature of existence is proclaimed as Brahman. (14)
That which is the unbroken form of the gods—this is the characteristic of a devotee.
(15) The Guru is the Liṅga; his command is the Śeṣa; the water from his feet is the Karūpaka.
That great reality which is vast and perfect is known as the Guru. (16)
That in which the visible world is dissolved is called the eternal *liṅga*.
It is held to be self-luminous by nature, consisting of existence (*sat*), consciousness (*cit*), and bliss (*ānanda*). This grace (*prasāda*) is distinguished by a hundredfold increase in happiness.
One whose consciousness has been made divine by the floods of the nectar of these [teachings] is called a devotee who has become one with that form.
His conduct consists of service to the Guru, his steadfastness is bound to the signs of that [divinity], and he is of that very nature. (18–19)
Listen to this water from the feet (pādodaka), which is pure knowledge, mobile, perceptible, and grace-bestowing; it is indeed of a single essence throughout.
This is the very nature of the fivefold conduct (pañcācāra) for one who possesses beginningless devotion.
Its characteristic is the sixfold conduct,
which is proclaimed as being in essence that very [Self], unbroken, full, eternal, and the light of consciousness;
it is supreme bliss and the essence of consciousness— this is the sixfold characteristic of the devotee.
O Goddess, hear now the sixfold characteristic of the Liṅga: it is full, eternal, the light of consciousness, supreme bliss, and the essence of consciousness;
it is the light of consciousness, full and eternal, and the supreme bliss that is the essence of consciousness. (23)
O Great Goddess, the state of being unfragmented has six kinds of moving characteristics.
In that which is full of supreme bliss, there is permanence, which is the manifestation of consciousness.
The essence of consciousness (cid-rasa) is indivisibility; its sixfold remaining characteristics are as follows:

O my beloved, the essence of existence (sad-rasa) is fullness, and the light of consciousness (cit-prakāśa) is supreme bliss—this is the sixfold indivisibility that constitutes the characteristic of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
This is the sixfold characteristic of his practice, consisting of the separate and mixed modes:
the Guru, the Liṅga, the Caru, the Prasāda, the water from the feet, the sacred ash, the Rudrākṣa beads, and the Mantra—these are said to be the limbs of the devotee. (27)
Prosperity is indeed the experience of the Supreme; bathing is immersion therein.
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is the absence of the three qualities (guṇas); though without marks, it is indeed the true mark.
Having made the mind, the face, and the senses into rudrākṣa beads, one should indeed wear them.
This wearing of rudrākṣas should be maintained according to fourteen stages.
In brief, the fivefold and sixfold principles do not perish.
That which is the five-syllabled mantra is itself the six-syllabled mantra.
Thus, his eightfold covering (āvaraṇa) is declared to be his eightfold reality (tattva).
The fivefold conduct, the sixfold form, and the eightfold covering—these constitute the eightfold body which, though distinct from his own essential nature, he bears. (31–32)
Indeed, this very nature belongs to one who has been devoted from time immemorial;
it is the form of all causes, as well as the supreme among all principles.
Listen now to this which has been declared regarding the nature of devotion from time immemorial.
To the one established in devotion, whose form is one's own inner state;
to the giver of the dwelling of supportless bliss;
to the bodiless, objectless, and senseless one.
In the resplendent, eternally abiding, and absolute state.
(34) This nature has been proclaimed for one who is devoted from time immemorial;
now, his status as the locus of the causal forms is being described. (35)
In the heart of one devoted from time immemorial, the Stainless One (Nirañjana) shines;

in the crest-lock (śikhā), the Liṅga of Emptiness; and in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the Sky of Consciousness (cidaṃbara). In the space between the eyebrows for the devotee of Śiva, and in the throat, there are indeed five powers (śaktis).
Thus there are the five Kalās and the five faces;
[there are] the five Sādākhyas, the five Nādas, and the five Mūrtis.
And within the Anāhata, his eight Īśvaras shine forth.
The Maṇipūraka-cakra has twenty-five forms;
in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, eleven Rudras are proclaimed for it. (39)
Upon its support reside Virāṭ, Antaryāmin, and Hiraṇyagarbha;
likewise, the ninefold divisions of Brahmā and the ten forms of Viṣṇu.
Thus indeed [is the state] of the beginningless devotee who dwells within the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) containing consciousness.
Those who have said "Thou art mine" are called *mūrvayas*; they are to be restrained, for they are the sources of the universe.
(41) Thus has been proclaimed the characteristic of one who is devoted from time immemorial.
He who is the beginningless, moving source abides in the western heart of the devotee. (42)
Its essential nature is now briefly revealed:
for one devoted to the animal [sacrifice] and others, it always resides within the heart-lotus,
situated in the midst of the seat of the *praṇava*, endowed with the support of the circle of consciousness.
The nature of that Praṇava is here declared to be "nirañjana" (stainless).
That which is devoid of "añjana"—the coloring [of the mind] manifested by the delusion of Māyā—is indeed "nirañjana" once it has been established in its true nature. || 44-45 ||
That very Brahman is partless, free from conceptual construction,
stainless, nameless, unrestrained, without need for food, and causeless; it is unattached,
without limiting adjuncts, incomparable, and actionless.

I worship that which is immovable, devoid of merit, without favor, and without excess; which is free from latent impressions, without end, beyond experience, and without rebirth—this stainless state, which is both that and its manifestation. 47.
The light devoid of beginning and end, the beginningless Lord, the imperishable;
indeed, the stainless one who is without instruction and without effort, the soul of all that is moving.
This is declared to be His supportless essential nature.
The four Vedas and the Purāṇas were within his womb;
all the yogis and sages took refuge at his feet, which are the source of all moving beings;
and within his body were all fourteen worlds.
From the soles of the feet up to the knees is known as Vitala; from the knees upward to the thighs is Sutala; at the region of the knees is Mahātala;
Talātala is in the thighs; and Rasātala is in the region of the private parts.
At the waist, however, Pātāla and the seven worlds are said to be situated:
Bhūrloka is in the middle of the belly, Bhuvarloka in the interior of the abdomen, Suvarloka in the heart, and Janarloka in the throat. (52–53)

From that [palate], the world of the ancestors (tālveśyā) arises; from the forehead, the world of sentient beings (satvaloka); and upon its crown is the Maharloka—thus the fourteen worlds are proclaimed. (54)
The cosmic egg is His crown; hear that His face is the sky.
All the directions are His arms, and the moon and sun are His eyes. His body is of the nature of space, and Vitala is the lotus of His feet.
The void-liṅga is in the palm of the hand; all clouds are heard as matted locks (jaṭā).
The moonlight is the sacred ash (vibhūti), and all the Vedas are my ritual actions (kriyā).
The stars are the flowers, and the principal mountain ranges are the rudrākṣa beads. || 56–57 ||
